article_title: Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents
citation: Sebastian P. Suggate, Viktoria L. Karle, Tanja Kipfelsberger, Heidrun Stoeger. (2025). Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents. Educational Research Review 49 (2025) 100748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100748
title: Four contrasting theoretical accounts of FMS–academic-cognitive links: amodal, maturation, functionalism, and shared processes
description: The article organises the fragmented theoretical literature into four contrasting accounts. Amodal theories see FMS as "simply the executors of centrally informed intentions" predicting no offline links; maturation attributes correlations to age variance; functionalism claims FMS "provide unique opportunities to engage in skillful actions that benefit academic learning"; and shared processes holds that FMS and cognitive skills draw on common neural and behavioural processes, including the nimble-hands nimble-minds hypothesis. The meta-analysis was designed to test these accounts against each other.
requirements: Correlational data covering FMS, academic skills, and cognitive skills simultaneously, enabling MASEM tests of direct versus mediated paths
constraints: The authors state their analyses "are certainly not sufficient for a final conclusion, especially since many of the theoretical approaches overlap"
examples: The meta-analysis tested amodal predictions via moderator control, maturation via age moderation, and functionalism versus shared processes via MASEM mediation comparison
key_sources: Sebastian P. Suggate, Viktoria L. Karle, Tanja Kipfelsberger, Heidrun Stoeger. (2025). Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents. Educational Research Review 49 (2025) 100748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100748

article_title: Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents
citation: Sebastian P. Suggate, Viktoria L. Karle, Tanja Kipfelsberger, Heidrun Stoeger. (2025). Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents. Educational Research Review 49 (2025) 100748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100748
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 118 FMS–academic-cognitive correlational studies (1110 effect sizes, N = 79,856)
description: A systematically assembled corpus of correlational studies linking fine motor skills to academic-cognitive skills in children aged 3–16, identified from 21,225 search hits across five databases and coded with interrater reliability of IRR = .98. It comprises 118 articles, 143 samples, and 1110 effect sizes, mostly cross-sectional (71.5%) and peer-reviewed (88.2%), with samples averaging 7.16 years (SD = 2.59). All meta-analytic data, analysis code, and coding materials are shared on OSF.
requirements: Studies reporting at least one correlation between a fine motor and an academic-cognitive measure, non-disabled samples aged 3–16, and no selective reporting of significant correlations
constraints: Excludes samples with diagnosed disability and children under three or over 16; correlational studies only, as FMS intervention studies were too few for meta-analysis
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 3–16 in mainstream educational settings
target_learning_goals: fine motor skills in relation to reading, writing, mathematics, and cognition
examples: Searches in May 2020 across PsycINFO, PubMed, MEDLINE, ERIC, and Web of Science; effect sizes reverse-coded so positive correlations always indicated better performance
key_sources: Sebastian P. Suggate, Viktoria L. Karle, Tanja Kipfelsberger, Heidrun Stoeger. (2025). Keep the hands in mind: A meta-analysis of correlations between fine motor skills and reading, writing, mathematics, and cognitive development in children and adolescents. Educational Research Review 49 (2025) 100748. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100748

article_title: Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.
citation: Alhadithi Ahmed, Almansour Mohammed. (2025). Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08489-6
title: FMLM Leadership and Management Standards for Undergraduate Medical Education
description: A comprehensive UK-based framework for UME derived from the UK Medical Leadership Competency Framework. It "outlined competencies across five domains: Demonstrating Personal Qualities, Working with Others, Managing Services, Improving Services, and Setting Direction." The framework describes MLM learning as integrated throughout the undergraduate program and reinforced across academic and clinical settings. It was the one non-peer-reviewed publication included in the review.
requirements: Designed as national-level guidance for UK undergraduate medical education
constraints: Provides broad direction for implementation but does not prescribe a single format
key_sources: Alhadithi Ahmed, Almansour Mohammed. (2025). Leadership and management competency frameworks in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08489-6

article_title: Fundamental motor skills, executive functions, and academic achievement of Chinese schoolchildren: Testing a mediating model.
citation: Wang Lijing, Sun Jiancui, Wang Lijuan, Zheng Danheng, Zhou Yulan. (2025). Fundamental motor skills, executive functions, and academic achievement of Chinese schoolchildren: Testing a mediating model. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0336470
title: Mediation model in which executive function transmits the effect of fundamental motor skills on academic achievement, grounded in Piaget's cognitive development theory
description: The article proposes and tests a hypothetical mediation model in which FMS (locomotor, object control, stability skills) is the independent variable, academic achievement (Chinese, mathematics) the dependent variable, and EF (working memory, inhibition control) the mediator, with paths a, b, c, and c' as shown in Fig 1. It is grounded in Piaget's view that "cognition is an individual's personal actions and interactions with the world", so physical movement supports cognitive development. The authors also invoke shared cognitive mechanisms and cerebellar–prefrontal cooperation as explanatory mechanisms, noting that "the cerebellum and the prefrontal cortex work together to activate and develop motor skills as well as cognitive functions".
requirements: The model requires measures of FMS components, EF components, and subject-specific academic achievement, with demographic covariates (age, gender, family income, mother's education) controlled.
constraints: The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; EF was measured by parental report, and the model excludes other potential mediators such as motivation, emotion knowledge, and physical fitness.
examples: The two SEM mediation models tested in this study (Chinese and mathematics) with bootstrapped confidence intervals constitute the model's empirical instantiation.
key_sources: Wang Lijing, Sun Jiancui, Wang Lijuan, Zheng Danheng, Zhou Yulan. (2025). Fundamental motor skills, executive functions, and academic achievement of Chinese schoolchildren: Testing a mediating model. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0336470

article_title: Perceived value of student-led near-peer teaching in anatomy education within a problem-based learning medical curriculum.
citation: Serhan Olivia, Girard Simon, Sylvestre Olivier. (2025). Perceived value of student-led near-peer teaching in anatomy education within a problem-based learning medical curriculum. Canadian Medical Education Journal, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.80274
title: FMSS Anatomy Club: a student-led near-peer virtual workshop program supplementing anatomy in a PBL medical curriculum
description: The FMSS Anatomy Club is a student-led near-peer teaching initiative founded by medical students at the University of Sherbrooke to bridge gaps in anatomy training under PBL. It "supplements preclinical education independently from the faculty" by "offering real-time virtual workshops" in which tutors just a few academic years ahead create a comfortable learning environment. In 2023-2024 it "conducted 11 workshops, with attendance varying between 40 and 160 participants".
requirements: Prospective tutors must show a strong anatomy foundation, favoring those with previous studies in the subject
Each workshop is collaboratively designed by three to four tutors, requiring on average 6-10 hours to develop
constraints: No formal training is provided for the tutors
Functions as a supplement independent from the faculty, which offers limited anatomy lab hours
target_learners: medical students in a problem-based learning undergraduate medical curriculum
target_learning_goals: anatomical knowledge of neuro-musculoskeletal and visceral concepts
examples: During the 2023-2024 academic year the club ran 11 workshops on topics including gastroenterology, upper and lower limbs, cardiovascular and respiratory systems, neurology, and genitourinary and vascular systems.
key_sources: Serhan Olivia, Girard Simon, Sylvestre Olivier. (2025). Perceived value of student-led near-peer teaching in anatomy education within a problem-based learning medical curriculum. Canadian Medical Education Journal, 16(4). https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.80274

article_title: Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners' beliefs.
citation: Vélez, N., Chen, A. M., Burke, T., Cushman, F. A., & Gershman, S. J. (2023). Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners’ beliefs. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2215015120
title: fMRI-adapted generalized teaching game with multiple-choice questions
description: A scanner task adapting classic teaching games such as the rectangle game to fMRI constraints. Teachers study a question of four 6 × 6 pixel drawings, then provide up to three examples by revealing light blue squares of the correct answer on a canvas, see the example from the learner's perspective, and rate how likely learners are to answer correctly. Questions were "designed to be sufficiently varied to prevent teachers from learning a simple strategy that would generalize across target concepts". Behavioral data, task code, and analysis code were deposited on Open Science Framework.
requirements: Teachers must be told their examples will be shown to future learners, and the question set must vary enough to prevent a cached rule such as touching opposite corners
constraints: Only positive examples contained within the target concept can be revealed, analogous to the constraint in past teaching games
target_learners: adult online learners tested on the provided examples
target_learning_goals: teaching abstract multiple-choice concepts through selected examples
examples: Twenty-eight participants taught 40 questions over 10 runs; 140 online learners were tested on the examples teachers provided, betting chips on the correct answer
key_sources: Vélez, N., Chen, A. M., Burke, T., Cushman, F. A., & Gershman, S. J. (2023). Teachers recruit mentalizing regions to represent learners’ beliefs. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2215015120

article_title: Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months.
citation: Bakwa Kanyinga Felly, Gogovor Amédé, Dofara Suélène Georgina, Gadio Souleymane, Tremblay Martin, Daniel Sam J., Rivest Louis-Paul, Légaré France. (2023). Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04597-3
title: Nine CPD courses at the FMSQ 2019 annual meeting, evaluated with a pre-post design and six-month follow-up
description: The study evaluated nine of 26 potentially eligible courses (9/26, 34.6%) offered as in-person didactic lectures at the FMSQ annual meeting on November 15, 2019 in Quebec City. Courses were eligible if the scientific committee agreed, the course "defined a main behavior change", and it targeted one of the seven CanMEDS roles. Of 329 attendees, 205 completed CPD-REACTION (62.3% response rate); 158 completed it before, 129 after, and 47 at six months; the population included 192 physicians, 40.6% female and 37.5% in surgical specialties.
requirements: Courses must define a main behavior change, target a CanMEDS role, and be accredited for inclusion in this evaluation approach
constraints: Sample size at individual course level was small; pooling courses was needed for statistical power, and loss to follow-up at six months was high (47/329)
target_learners: medical specialist physicians across surgical, laboratory and medical specialties
target_learning_goals: adoption of targeted clinical behaviors defined by each CPD course
examples: Course topics included patient safety, care incidents, optimization of care, perioperative pain and opioids, sports injuries, eating disorders, ADHD, cardio-oncology and local anesthesia.
key_sources: Bakwa Kanyinga Felly, Gogovor Amédé, Dofara Suélène Georgina, Gadio Souleymane, Tremblay Martin, Daniel Sam J., Rivest Louis-Paul, Légaré France. (2023). Evaluating the impact of continuing professional development courses on physician behavioral intention: a pre-post study with follow-up at six months. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04597-3

article_title: Evaluation of Situational Judgment Tests in student selection in Indonesia and the impact on diversity issues.
citation: Soemantri Diantha, Findyartini Ardi, Yolanda Sophie, Morley Emma, Patterson Fiona. (2022). Evaluation of Situational Judgment Tests in student selection in Indonesia and the impact on diversity issues. BMC Medical Education, 22:239. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03247-4
title: FMUI situational judgment test assessing non-academic attributes for medical student selection
description: A knowledge-based instruction situational judgment test developed at the Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Indonesia to assess non-academic attributes in admissions. Each scenario is "a short paragraph (approximately 50–100 words to reduce cognitive load)" followed by five to eight responses rated from very appropriate to very inappropriate; scoring rewards proximity to an expert consensus key, with a maximum possible score of 512.
requirements: Scenarios set in healthcare/learning contexts and answerable by high school leaver candidates
An expert concordance stage with a minimum of 70% agreement to define the scoring key
constraints: Piloted at a single institution; SJT items belong to the institution and are not to be released
target_learners: high school leaver applicants to undergraduate medical school
examples: 30 scenarios comprising 128 nested items were piloted with two applicant cohorts completing the paper-based SJT for 1 h under invigilated exam conditions
key_sources: Soemantri Diantha, Findyartini Ardi, Yolanda Sophie, Morley Emma, Patterson Fiona. (2022). Evaluation of Situational Judgment Tests in student selection in Indonesia and the impact on diversity issues. BMC Medical Education, 22:239. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03247-4
